title: Atrial fibrillation
summary: Rapid, disorganised wavelets, often triggered at the pulmonary veins, activate the atria. The ventricular response is irregularly irregular.

events.label: Pulmonary vein trigger
events.caption: Rapid firing from the pulmonary veins (tinted) starts the arrhythmia. The sleeves of atrial muscle around the veins are the usual triggers. Other atrial sites join in.
events.ecg: The baseline begins to look irregular.

events.label: Disorganised activation
events.caption: New impulses arrive before the atria have fully recovered, so each activates only the tissue that is ready. Wavefronts collide and fragment: there is no single organised wave. The atrial rate is 400 to 600 per minute.
events.ecg: Fibrillatory waves, small, fast and varying in shape, instead of P waves.

events.label: AV node filters
events.caption: The AV node is bombarded and conducts only some impulses, at irregular intervals, depending on how recovered it is.
events.ecg: Narrow QRS complexes at irregular intervals.

events.label: Irregularly irregular
events.caption: The ventricular rhythm has no pattern. Compare the R-R intervals.
events.ecg: An irregularly irregular narrow-complex rhythm with no P waves.

teaching_points: Atrial fibrillation: rapid, disorganised atrial activity at 400-600 per minute from multiple foci or wavefronts, with an irregularly irregular ventricular response.
Pulmonary vein triggers are the target of catheter ablation (pulmonary vein isolation).
It is not the only irregular narrow-complex tachycardia: ectopics, multifocal atrial tachycardia and flutter with variable block can mimic it.
